A Case for Crown and Continuity: Re-establishing a Hereditary Monarchy in the United States

I. Preliminary objections—and why they are weaker than they first appear
Every American instinctively recoils at the word “king.” Our civic memory centers, quite literally, on a rejection of monarchy. Yet history is full of ideas once discarded that later proved worth resuming. The Roman Republic abandoned kings at its birth, only to discover, centuries later, that stable rule under a single princeps was preferable to chronic civil war. Today we revere Washington more for relinquishing power than for wielding it; still, we forget that his contemporaries considered crowning him “King George I of America.” That proposal failed by a vote of only three colonies. Given the chronic volatility, polarization, and institutional fatigue now afflicting our republic, the old idea is due for a new hearing—not out of nostalgia, but out of sober realism about what best secures liberty and common purpose over time.

II. Defining the proposal precisely
The monarchy advanced here is not personal dictatorship or divine-right absolutism. It is a 21st-century adaptation: a hereditary, ceremonial head of state serving for life, but wholly above electoral competition, stripped of day-to-day executive power. Legislative authority would remain in Congress, adjudicative authority in the courts—the separation of powers preserved, merely with a king (or queen) in place of a president as symbolic sovereign. Among the most robust constitutional monarchies—Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Japan—reigning houses endure precisely by fusing tradition with modern constraints. Such a hybrid model can be custom-built to American principles, retaining a written constitution, an independent press, and full civil liberties.

III. Ending the four-year demolition derby
Every election cycle now resembles an existential showdown. Policymaking halts eighteen months before each vote; governing programs swing wildly every four to eight years; presidents enter office already looking to “win” the next election rather than govern. A hereditary monarch ends this treadmill. Because succession is automatic, the head of state can think in terms of decades, even centuries. Long-term problems—the national debt, climate transition, deteriorating infrastructure—can be framed and safeguarded by a figure whose horizon extends far beyond any election.

IV. Liberating policy from personality
Ambitious individuals no longer campaign for the Crown, which means that personality cults can no longer dominate public life. A monarch is born into office; campaigning dies at the palace gates. Politics shrinks to its proper sphere—arguments over policy, not over who best pretends to “feel our pain.” The short-term benefit is liberation from the chronic fund-raising, polling, and media manipulation required of presidential hopefuls. The long-term benefit is cultivation of political modesty: losing an election ceases to resemble losing national identity when the unifying symbol of the nation—the Crown—stands beyond partisan capture.

V. Constitutional guardrails, not parliamentary absolutes
Critics need not fear some mythical return to Stuart tyranny. A written constitution—ratified by supermajority after full national deliberation—would specify inviolable boundaries: no royal edicts, no veto except on constitutional advice of the High Court, no power of the purse, no command of troops in war without congressional declaration. No monarch may sit in either chamber of Congress. Impeachment power remains, but by a two-thirds vote of both Houses plus a majority in three-quarters of state legislatures—high bar, yet reachable if royal conduct should turn egregious. Succession laws would be fixed by statute a generation in advance, removing caprice from genetic misfortune; abdication could occur only by personal renunciation plus assent from Congress.

VI. Economic transparency via a fixed civil list
Opponents often invoke cost. Yet the present presidency consumes billions: Air Force One, Secret Service details for life, multiple secure residences, transition staffs every four to eight years, and a sprawling White House bureaucracy whose size expands with each administration. Constitutional monarchies operate at drastically lower cost: the Dutch monarchy’s annual budget equals roughly one hour of United States federal outlays. A fixed civil list, publicly audited, housing a single royal household occupying one residence (perhaps a modest wing of the existing White House) replaces a rolling carnival that devours more every decade. The crown would not own assets privately; historic estates revert to the public trust.

VII. Rescue of the civic imagination
Monarchy alone among modern institutions provides a bearer of national memory whose genealogy literally lengthens through living generations. Americans crave permanence amid manic change. The Fourth of July parades gradually mingle into Thanksgiving shopping; veterans pass away without a visible focal tie to the young. A monarch embodies continuity: every birthday parade, every state opening of Congress, every moment of national mourning proclaims that this republic lives within an unbroken story. Patriotism migrates from ideology to inheritance: the citizen and the sovereign belong to the same cross-generational project.

VIII. Non-partisan diplomacy and soft power abroad
Presidents arrive on the global stage as representatives of transient political coalitions, their handshakes shadowed by party baggage. A king or queen forever avoids domestic factions, can therefore serve as untainted envoy, more easily brokering peace or delivering humanitarian messages. Constitutional monarchs function as super-ambassadors: Queen Elizabeth II opened doors no prime minister could; Carl XVI Gustaf quietly defused Arctic disputes where Swedish partisans dared not tread. The United States, late in Empire yet feebler in goodwill, could redirect vast presidential travel budgets into a single, impeccably trained royal diplomatic corps, whose very neutrality becomes a strategic asset.

IX. The racial and ethnic question honestly confronted
Some fear monarchy as reactionary because it seems rooted in old European bloodlines. But succession law, like the Constitution itself, must be freely chosen. Americans could legally stipulate that the first monarch descend from a line that embodies the national mix: perhaps the great-great grandchild of Martin Luther King Jr. merged into the line of a native nation—or perhaps we establish rotation among several noble houses elected by supermajorities in Congress for lifetime thrones, yet hereditary within each selected line. There is nothing inevitable about Eurocentric or dynastic whiteness. Monarchy is moldable; elections have not, in truth, solved American racism, and may indeed have intensified it.

X. Historical precedents on our own soil
We already live with quasi-hereditary rule at the state level: in the Roosevelts, the Kennedys, the Bushes, the Cheneys, the Browns of California, the Longs of Louisiana. The difference is that these dynasties court votes rather than embody continuity. Neighboring Canada, rooted in the same British legal tradition we once shared, has sustained constitutional monarchy for 157 years within federalism, free speech, and multilingual democracy. Australia likewise. Their debates reveal grievances, sometimes republican flare-ups, but even their republican proponents concede the practical difficulty of improving upon the system they presently possess.

XI. Addressing the fear of stagnation
Skeptics claim that an un-elected sovereign would slow social reform. Yet monarchs do not hold policy veto in any modern model. Sweden and Spain both leapt into social-democratic modernity while retaining royals. Canada legislated universal health care and marriage equality with a queen on the currency. Progress comes from parliaments and courts, mobilized, if anything, by a publicly esteemed neutral head of state who arbitrates crises without threatening the gains of reformers.

XII. Transition mechanism
The passage would be peaceful, constitutional, reversible:

  1. A two-thirds vote in both Houses of Congress and ratification by three-quarters of states ordain the amendment establishing “a sovereign of the United States.”
  2. The amendment creates a Regency Council that, within six months, appoints the first monarch by a unanimous choice reflecting plural national heritage, adoption into symbolic bloodline by act of Parliament, and formal enthronement in Independence Hall, Philadelphia.
  3. Simultaneously the amendment sunsets the office of president on January 20 of the fourth year after ratification, transferring executive command to a prime-ministerial cabinet chosen by the House.
  4. Two subsequent national plebiscites—one at ten years, one at twenty—allow simple majority vote to restore the presidency if majorities so demand. Reversibility guarantees democratic experimentalism.

XIII. Conclusion: Monarchy as liberty’s shield, not its grave
The genius of liberty does not reside in perpetual plebiscites, but in the civic architecture that prevents any faction from becoming oppressor. A hereditary monarch, checked, confined, and constitutional, offers a paradox: the least powerful citizen becomes sovereign for life, yet shackled by law; the most ambitious politician no longer commandeers national identity for partisan ends; and the American people, without having to vote every four years on their very identity, are freed to argue—as citizens in robust republics always have—not about who rules, but about what is just.

George Washington’s republic triumphed in its century. The twenty-first century requires defense not merely against tyrants, but against fractured memory, corrosive cynicism, and institutional burnout. A crown may sound antique. Yet the true American spirit is not one of mindless novelty, but of pragmatic choice. We once chose to be a republic; nothing prevents us from choosing—not mythic kingship, but a reasoned, modern crown that conserves liberty by resting above its storms. In a time of eroding faith and endless campaign warfare, the continuity of a constitutional monarch may be the only lever durable enough to re-anchor the promise of e pluribus unum.

The Case for a Constitutional Hereditary Monarchy in the United States

The United States today suffers from a terminal case of institutional paralysis. Partisan gridlock, policy whiplash with every election cycle, and the spectacle of leaders chosen through increasingly vicious popularity contests have eroded national cohesion and long-range competence. Replacing the office of the elected president with a hereditary constitutional monarch as permanent, non-partisan head of state would restore stability, elevate the nation above factional warfare, and realign leadership with the demands of a complex modern society. This is not a call for absolute kingship but for a strictly limited sovereign, bound by a robust constitution and an elected legislature, modeled on the successful systems that have endured in Britain, Japan, and the Nordic countries. America’s experiment with an elected executive as both symbol and operator has failed its own test of time; a monarchy would correct the structural defects without sacrificing democratic accountability in governance.

The presidency’s biennial and quadrennial convulsions impose constant uncertainty on national affairs. Each new administration treats its predecessor’s major initiatives as reversibles, canceling treaties, regulatory frameworks, and infrastructure projects simply because they originated on the other side of the aisle. This short-termism wastes trillions and discourages the multi-decade investments required for energy, transportation, and defense. A hereditary monarch, by contrast, embodies continuity across generations. Succession occurs within the family line according to established rules, typically at the death of the incumbent rather than through national convulsions. The sovereign’s tenure spans decades without regard to electoral calendars, compelling policymakers to consider legacies that outlast any single career. Historical parallels confirm the pattern: while American governments have lurched from expansion to contraction on tax policy, trade, and military posture with each partisan turnover, constitutional monarchies have maintained steadier strategic horizons, evident in Britain’s consistent approach to alliances despite frequent prime ministerial changes.

Partisanship has consumed the head of state role. An elected president enters office as the champion of one coalition and remains its prisoner. Appointments, pardons, and even ceremonial functions carry the stain of that origin, so that roughly half the population views the office as alien or hostile. A monarch severs this link. As head of state above politics, the sovereign performs unifying functions—receiving foreign dignitaries, signing laws, opening legislative sessions, and representing the country in moments of tragedy or triumph—without having campaigned on divisive platforms. This separation leaves the prime minister or equivalent elected executive to absorb the heat of policy battles while the crown serves as neutral arbiter and national conscience. In practice, this arrangement reduces the personalization of the constitution. Scandals attach to the government of the day rather than permanently damaging the enduring symbol of the state. Public trust data from established monarchies shows sustained higher confidence in the ceremonial head than in transient political figures, a buffer the United States demonstrably lacks.

Preparation for the role further favors heredity over electoral selection. A future monarch can be raised from childhood with exhaustive training in history, constitutional law, diplomacy, and economics, free from the requirement to win votes by flattering transient popular sentiments. This grooming produces a specialist in the long view rather than a generalist politician adept at sound bites. Counterexamples from republican systems abound: many presidents arrive in office with narrow experience in one domain and little prior acquaintance with the full machinery of statecraft. While poor monarchs have existed, the hereditary pipeline allows for the identification and sidelining of unsuitable heirs through constitutional mechanisms—regencies, parliamentary intervention, or abdication—without subjecting the entire nation to the circus of impeachment or recall. Modern European dynasties demonstrate that rigorous education combined with public scrutiny produces competent stewards far more often than random electoral chemistry.

Critics rightly note that America’s founding rejected monarchy, but that rejection targeted absolute, unaccountable power rather than the limited, symbolic variety now proposed. The framers feared tyranny from a distant or hereditary ruler who could ignore representative bodies. A contemporary American monarchy would operate under a written constitution that reserves all legislative, budgetary, and appointment authority to an elected Congress and executive government. The monarch’s powers would mirror those of the British sovereign: the right to be consulted, to encourage, and to warn—advisory rather than directive. This framework preserves popular sovereignty while insulating the head of state from the democratic process’s tendency to elevate showmen over statesmen. Far from contradicting republican principles, constitutional monarchy refines them by introducing an element immune to the short-cycle incentives that distort elected leadership.

Implementation would require a constitutional amendment establishing the office and selecting the initial dynasty through a deliberative process, perhaps drawing from distinguished military, academic, or civic lineages to launch the line. Thereafter, succession passes automatically to the nearest heir meeting competency standards set by statute. The existing presidential residence could become the royal palace with ceremonial modification, while an elected prime minister assumes day-to-day executive responsibilities. Cost concerns are misplaced; many monarchies spend less on the head of state than the United States currently allocates to the presidencies’s trappings, security apparatus, and perpetual campaigning infrastructure. The symbolic return, including enhanced diplomatic leverage through lifelong relationships and neutral mediation during domestic crises, outweighs any marginal outlay.

The United States has reached the point where its political class’s addiction to permanent conflict threatens its cohesion. A hereditary constitutional monarch would furnish the missing fixed point in that system—an impartial representative of the whole people whose sole interest lies in the endurance of the nation itself. This reform neither ends democracy nor revives feudalism; it applies a proven corrective to the specific defects of an elected executive who must perpetually divide the country to sustain power. The resulting architecture would deliver greater continuity, elevated national symbolism, and a clearer separation of partisan combat from institutional stability. Democracy may not be perfect, but as Winston Churchill observed, it is the worst form of government except for all the others that have been tried. After more than two centuries of elected presidencies, we still watch the same cycle repeat: polarization hardens into permanent camps, elections reward the most relentless rhetoricians rather than the most steadied stewards, and the presidency—by design a politically chosen office—absorbs the anger and urgency of every disagreement. 1) A head of state should unite the nation, not campaign for it

In most democracies, there is a sharp difference between governing and representing. Legislatures govern through laws and oversight. Governments execute those laws. The American presidential system—especially when paired with strong party discipline—creates winner-take-all incentives. Critics often assume “hereditary monarchy” automatically implies unchecked power. That is neither logically necessary nor historically inevitable. In short, consent can be updated. The system’s legitimacy would come from lawful constitutional adoption and continued democratic governance, not from the monarch’s campaign ability.

The United States does not lack democracy; it lacks a stabilizing constitutional symbol that stands above party conflict. The elected presidency, while meaningful, structurally invites polarization because the head of state must campaign and represent party victory. That arrangement makes national legitimacy feel temporary and contested. It also concentrates incentives for electoral combat into the center of the executive branch.

Reestablishing a constitutional hereditary monarchy offers an alternative designed for modern constitutional democracy: a permanent, nonpartisan head of state who embodies continuity, reduces the emotional stakes of elections, and helps stabilize the political environment—while elected representatives and accountable government continue to govern day-to-day affairs. Far from undermining liberty, a properly constrained monarchy can reinforce limited government through constitutional design, judicial oversight, and strict limits on royal power.

In an era of unprecedented political polarization, governmental gridlock, and declining faith in democratic institutions, perhaps it is time for Americans to consider a radical reimagining of our system of government. The Crisis of the Current System

The American presidency has evolved far beyond what the Founders envisioned. Originally conceived as a relatively weak executive subordinate to Congress, the presidency has accumulated enormous power while simultaneously becoming a lightning rod for partisan hatred. Every four years, the nation endures an exhausting, expensive, and divisive election cycle that leaves roughly half the country feeling disenfranchised. The president must simultaneously be a unifying national symbol and a partisan political operator. This dual role inevitably fails, as political decisions necessarily alienate large portions of the population who then reject the president's legitimacy as a national representative.

The Monarchical Solution

A hereditary constitutional monarchy would elegantly solve these systemic problems. By separating the roles of head of state (the monarch) and head of government (an elected prime minister), we could preserve democratic governance while providing stable, non-partisan national leadership. The monarch would serve as a unifying figure above politics, performing ceremonial duties, providing constitutional continuity, and representing the nation's values and traditions.

Consider the success of constitutional monarchies worldwide. Nations like Canada, the United Kingdom, Japan, and the Scandinavian countries consistently rank among the world's most stable, prosperous, and democratic societies. Their monarchs provide a focal point for national unity while elected parliaments handle day-to-day governance. These countries enjoy lower political polarization, as the most visible national figure remains politically neutral.

Advantages of Hereditary Succession

While hereditary succession may seem arbitrary to modern sensibilities, it offers unique advantages. A future monarch raised from birth for their role receives decades of preparation in diplomacy, constitutional law, and public service. Compare this to presidents who often assume office with little experience and spend their first years learning on the job. Monarchs, serving for life, can take a long-term perspective impossible for politicians focused on the next election cycle.

Furthermore, hereditary succession removes the corrupting influence of political ambition. A monarch who inherits their position need not make promises to special interests or compromise their principles for electoral success. They can serve as a truly independent guardian of constitutional norms and democratic procedures.

Economic and Practical Benefits

Critics might cite the cost of maintaining a royal family, but constitutional monarchies often prove economically beneficial. The British Royal Family, for instance, generates far more in tourism revenue than it costs to maintain. An American royal family could similarly become a source of fascination and economic activity, attracting visitors to royal palaces and ceremonies.

Moreover, imagine the savings from eliminating presidential elections, which now cost billions of dollars and produce months of economic uncertainty. These resources could be redirected to education, infrastructure, or other productive uses rather than attack advertisements and campaign consultants.

The Constitutional Path Forward

Admittedly, establishing an American monarchy would require a constitutional amendment—a deliberately difficult process. However, this high bar ensures that such a transformation would only occur with overwhelming popular support. The amendment could carefully circumscribe royal powers, ensuring the monarch remains a figurehead with no ability to interfere in democratic governance.

As for selecting the first monarch, various approaches exist. We might look to descendants of George Washington, honoring our first president by establishing his line as our royal family. Alternatively, we could select from among distinguished families who have served the nation across generations—perhaps the Adams, Roosevelt, or Kennedy families.

Addressing Common Objections

Critics will invoke the Revolution and claim monarchy contradicts American values. Yet the Founders rebelled against absolute monarchy, not constitutional monarchy. They sought representation and limited government—goals entirely compatible with modern constitutional monarchism. Indeed, Canada achieved these same goals while retaining the Crown.

Others worry about creating an entrenched aristocracy. However, modern constitutional monarchies have proven more egalitarian than the United States, with its growing wealth inequality and informal aristocracy of political dynasties. A clearly defined royal family with circumscribed privileges might prove less threatening to equality than our current system of unlimited wealth accumulation and political influence.

Conclusion

The United States faces a choice between continuing down a path of increasing polarization and governmental dysfunction or boldly reimagining our institutions for the challenges ahead. A constitutional monarchy offers proven benefits: political stability, national unity, long-term planning, and freedom from permanent campaigning. By elevating a hereditary monarch as our non-partisan head of state, we could heal our divisions while preserving—indeed strengthening—our democratic institutions.

The Crown could become a symbol of what unites us rather than what divides us, a guardian of our Constitution rather than a threat to it, and a source of stability in an uncertain world. As we approach our nation's 250th anniversary, perhaps it is time to complete our constitutional evolution by embracing the crowned republic model that has served other democracies so well. In doing so, we would not betray our revolutionary heritage but fulfill it, creating a more perfect union that could endure for centuries to come.

The Case for a Hereditary Monarchy in the United States: Stability, Unity, and a Return to Constitutional Sovereignty

Introduction

The United States was founded on the principle of limited government, where power is carefully balanced to prevent tyranny. Yet, over the centuries, the American political system has devolved into a dysfunctional, hyper-partisan, and increasingly unstable presidency—one that has become a magnet for corruption, populist demagoguery, and the erosion of constitutional norms. The solution? A return to the time-tested institution of hereditary monarchy, where a permanent, non-partisan, and constitutionally constrained head of state—rather than an elected president—serves as the symbolic and ceremonial unifier of the nation.

While the idea may seem radical to modern ears, a hereditary monarchy would restore stability, national unity, and constitutional integrity—values that the current presidential system has systematically undermined. By removing the presidency from the realm of partisan politics, we could end the cycle of divisive elections, executive overreach, and the dangerous concentration of power in the hands of a single, fallible individual. A king or queen, bound by tradition, law, and an unbroken lineage, would serve as a neutral arbiter of the nation’s identity, ensuring that America remains a republic in the truest sense: a government of laws, not of men.

This essay will argue that a hereditary monarchy is not only practical and beneficial for the United States but also necessary to preserve the principles upon which the nation was founded.

I. The Failures of the Presidential System: Why We Need a Change

The American presidency, once a model of restrained executive power, has become a source of instability, corruption, and constitutional crisis. The flaws of the current system are undeniable:

A. The Tyranny of the Two-Year Election Cycle

The presidency is now hostage to the whims of public opinion, forcing leaders to govern through the lens of short-term political survival rather than long-term national interest. Every two years, Congress becomes a battleground, and every four years, the presidency is up for grabs in a spectacle of mud-slinging, misinformation, and demagoguery.

  • Example: The 2016 and 2020 elections were not contests of policy but culture wars, with deepening polarization and violent rhetoric (e.g., the January 6 Capitol riot).
  • Result: Presidents avoid difficult but necessary decisions (e.g., entitlement reform, military withdrawal, or diplomatic concessions) for fear of political backlash.
  • Solution: A hereditary monarch, elected by no one and answerable to no political faction, would govern with long-term vision, free from the tyranny of the ballot box.

B. Executive Overreach and the Erosion of Checks and Balances

The Founding Fathers designed the presidency to be weak compared to Congress, but over time, executive power has expanded beyond recognition.

  • Examples of Overreach:

    • War Powers: Presidents (from Truman to Obama to Trump) have unilaterally committed the U.S. to wars without congressional approval (e.g., Korea, Vietnam, Iraq, Libya, Syria).
    • Executive Orders: Presidents now bypass Congress with sweeping decrees (e.g., Obama’s DACA, Trump’s travel bans, Biden’s student debt relief).
    • Emergency Powers: The Insurrection Act (1807) and National Emergencies Act (1976) have been abused to justify martial law-like measures (e.g., Trump’s deployment of troops at the border, Biden’s COVID mandates).
    • Judicial Appointments: The packing of the federal courts (especially the Supreme Court) has turned the judiciary into a political weapon rather than an impartial arbiter.

  • Result: The presidency has become more like a monarchy—but a weak, unstable, and partisan one, where power is concentrated in the hands of a single, elected individual rather than a constitutionally constrained hereditary line.

  • Solution: A hereditary monarch would be bound by tradition and law, preventing the kind of unchecked power grabs that have plagued modern presidencies.

C. The Corrupting Influence of Money and Partisanship

The presidential system is fundamentally corruptible because it rewards political operatives, not statesmen.

  • Campaign Finance: The two-party duopoly ensures that only the wealthy or those backed by corporate interests can realistically run for president. The 2020 election cost over $14 billion—a sum that distorts policy in favor of donors.

  • Lobbying and Revolving Door: Former presidents, vice presidents, and cabinet members cash in on their connections, creating a permanent political-industrial complex (e.g., Trump’s post-presidency business deals, Biden’s family’s foreign entanglements).

  • Partisan Gridlock: The two-party system ensures that no meaningful compromise is possible, leading to government shutdowns, debt ceiling crises, and legislative paralysis.

  • Result: The presidency is no longer a meritocracy of leadership but a contest of wealth, media savvy, and partisan loyalty.

  • Solution: A hereditary monarch would transcend party politics, serving as a neutral figurehead who does not campaign, does not fundraise, and does not owe allegiance to any faction.

D. The Danger of Demagoguery and Populist Tyranny

The presidential system rewards charismatic but dangerous leaders who exploit fear, nationalism, and anti-establishment rhetoric.

  • Examples:

    • Andrew Jackson (1829–1837) – Used populist appeals to expand executive power, ignore the Supreme Court (Trail of Tears), and destroy the national bank.
    • Woodrow Wilson (1913–1921) – Suspended civil liberties during WWI, jailed political opponents, and pushed for a League of Nations despite constitutional objections.
    • Franklin D. Roosevelt (1933–1945) – Packed the Supreme Court, imprisoned Japanese-Americans, and expanded executive authority under the New Deal.
    • Donald Trump (2017–2021) – Attacked the press as "the enemy of the people," encouraged political violence, and tried to overturn an election.
    • Joe Biden (2021–present) – Uses executive orders to bypass Congress, deports record numbers of migrants, and faces growing allegations of cognitive decline.

  • Result: The most unstable and dangerous leaders are often the most electable because they play to the emotions of the masses.

  • Solution: A hereditary monarch would not be elected, meaning no demagogue could seize power through populist appeals. Instead, leadership would be based on lineage, training, and constitutional duty—not charisma or mob appeal.

II. The Benefits of a Hereditary Monarchy: Stability, Unity, and Constitutional Sovereignty

A hereditary monarchy would restore balance to the American system by separating the head of state from the head of government, ensuring that no single individual accumulates too much power.

A. A Permanent, Non-Partisan Head of State

Unlike a president, who is tied to a political party and a four-year term, a monarch would serve for life, ensuring continuity and stability.

  • No More "Lame Duck" Presidents: A monarch does not face re-election, meaning no last-minute policy shifts (e.g., Obama’s Iran Deal, Trump’s pardon spree).
  • No More Transition Chaos: A smooth handover of power (as seen in the UK’s monarchy) would prevent the kind of political upheaval we saw after the 2020 election.
  • No More Partisan Gridlock: Since the monarch does not belong to any party, they could serve as a unifying figure, above the fray of Democratic vs. Republican squabbling.

B. A Check on Executive Power

Under a monarchy, the president (or prime minister, if we adopt a parliamentary system) would be subordinate to the crown, preventing executive overreach.

  • Veto Power: The monarch could veto unconstitutional laws (as the British monarch technically can, though rarely does).
  • Appointment of Ministers: The monarch could approve or reject cabinet appointments, ensuring competent, non-corrupt officials.
  • Emergency Powers: The monarch could refuse to declare martial law unless absolutely necessary, preventing presidential dictatorships.

C. A Symbol of National Unity

The U.S. is deeply divided—between red and blue states, urban and rural areas, rich and poor. A monarch could serve as a unifying symbol, above the culture wars.

  • Example: The British Royal Family remains popular despite political scandals because it transcends party politics.
  • Result: A ceremonial monarch could reunite the nation under a shared national identity, rather than tribal partisan loyalty.

D. A Return to Constitutional Government

The Founding Fathers feared a strong executive—that’s why they limited the president’s term to four years and denied re-election. Yet, over time, the presidency has become the most powerful office in the world.

A monarchy would restore the balance of power by:

  • Weakening the presidency (making it more like a prime minister, accountable to Congress).
  • Strengthening Congress (since the monarch would not interfere in legislation).
  • Protecting the judiciary (since the monarch would not appoint judges for political reasons).

E. Economic and Diplomatic Benefits

A monarchy would stabilize American foreign policy and boost the economy by:

  • Ending the "America First" vs. "Globalist" divide – A monarch would prioritize long-term national interest, not short-term political gains.
  • Attracting foreign investment – A stable, hereditary leadership would reduce geopolitical risk, making the U.S. more attractive to global markets.
  • Strengthening alliances – A permanent head of state would build deeper diplomatic ties with other monarchies (UK, Japan, Saudi Arabia, etc.).

III. Objections and Rebuttals

Objection 1: "Monarchy is Undemocratic!"

Rebuttal:

  • Democracy does not require direct election of the head of state. Many democracies (e.g., Germany, India, Israel) have ceremonial presidents who are not elected by popular vote.
  • The U.S. already has an undemocratic element—the Electoral College—which gives small states disproportionate power.
  • A monarchy would actually be more democratic in the long run because it removes the presidency from partisan politics, ensuring stable, competent leadership rather than populist demagogues.

Objection 2: "What if the monarch is incompetent or corrupt?"

Rebuttal:

  • Hereditary monarchs are trained from birth to fulfill their role. The British Royal Family has centuries of experience in ceremonial duties.
  • Constitutional constraints would prevent abuse (e.g., the monarch cannot veto laws arbitrarily, as they are bound by tradition and law).
  • If a monarch were truly unfit, parliament could intervene (as happened with King Edward VIII’s abdication in 1936).

Objection 3: "The U.S. was founded to reject monarchy!"

Rebuttal:

  • The Founding Fathers did not reject monarchy outright—they rejected tyranny.
  • Many Founders (e.g., Washington, Adams, Hamilton) admired constitutional monarchy.
  • The U.S. already has a "monarch" in the form of the president—a single, unelected (by the people) leader with vast, unchecked power.
  • A hereditary monarchy would actually be more in line with the Founders' vision because it separates the head of state from the head of government, preventing executive tyranny.

Objection 4: "It’s too radical—Americans would never accept it!"

Rebuttal:

  • Radical changes are sometimes necessary to prevent collapse. The American Revolution itself was radical—yet it succeeded.
  • Public opinion can be shaped through education and debate. Many once-unthinkable ideas (e.g., women’s suffrage, civil rights, same-sex marriage) became mainstream.
  • If the alternative is continued political instability, corruption, and demagoguery, then monarchy may be the least radical option.

Conclusion: A Monarch for a New American Century

The American presidential system has failed. It has concentrated too much power in the hands of a single, fallible individual, fueled partisan warfare, and enabled demagogues to rise to power. The solution is not more democracy—it is less democracy in the wrong places.

A hereditary monarchy would: ✅ End the tyranny of the two-year election cycle ✅ Prevent executive overreach and tyranny ✅ Transcend partisan politics ✅ Restore stability and national unity ✅ Strengthen constitutional government

The Founding Fathers feared a strong executive—yet today, the presidency is the strongest office in the world. It is time to return to their original vision: a republic with a ceremonial monarch, where power is balanced, leadership is stable, and the nation is united.

The question is not whether America should become a monarchy—but how soon we can make it happen. The alternative is continued decline, division, and the slow death of the republic. The choice is clear: A king or queen for a new American century.

In Defense of the Crown: An Argument for Restoring the Monarchy in America

I. Introduction: A Question We Should Not Dismiss

The American Revolution was fought in the name of liberty, but the men who led it were not unified in their rejection of monarchy. Alexander Hamilton openly admired the British constitutional model; John Adams drafted a proposal for a hereditary upper chamber; George Washington was offered a crown and declined only on the grounds that the moment was not right. Two hundred and fifty years later, with the partisan machinery of the Republic grinding ever more viciously, with elections consuming billions of dollars and dividing households, with presidents cycling through scandals, impeachments, and culture-war firestorms every four years, it is worth asking a question the Founders themselves wrestled with: was the rejection of hereditary monarchy a principle, or merely a convenience of 1776? A serious case can be made that the time has come to reestablish a constitutional monarchy in the United States, with a sovereign king or queen serving as the permanent, non-partisan head of state above the fray of electoral politics.

II. The Monarchy as a Non-Partisan Unifier

The single greatest virtue of a constitutional monarchy is the one Americans most conspicuously lack: a head of state who belongs to no party, no faction, and no political moment. The President of the United States is, by constitutional design, a partisan. He is elected by one party, embodies that party's ideology, appoints judges and officials from that party, and is succeeded by the other party, who will systematically reverse his work. The result is a perpetual cultural war fought in four-year spasms.

A monarch, by contrast, reigns for life. The British sovereign, the King of Sweden, the Emperor of Japan — these figures are not Republicans or Democrats, not conservatives or liberals. They are symbols of the nation entire. When a tragedy strikes, when a national holiday is observed, when a foreign dignitary arrives, the monarch is the figure to whom all citizens can look without the suspicion that they are being conscripted into a political faction. Americans today have no such figure. They have a President who polarizes by definition.

The genius of the constitutional monarchy, as practiced in Scandinavia, the Low Countries, the United Kingdom, Japan, and the Commonwealth realms, is that it separates symbolic representation from political governance. The monarch reigns; the elected parliament rules. The monarch is the head of state; the prime minister is the head of government. This division has produced some of the most stable, prosperous, and contented democracies on earth.

III. Continuity, Stability, and the Long View

A republic elects a president. A monarchy raises a king. The difference is profound.

An elected leader governs for a season, and his every thought is bent on the next election. A monarch governs for a generation, and his every thought ought to be bent on the long-term welfare of the realm, the education of his heir, the preservation of institutions, the cultivation of national character over decades. There is no incentive for a hereditary sovereign to slash the forests for short-term gain, to debase the currency for electoral advantage, to wage war for a news cycle. The king's children will inherit the consequences. This is not a sentimental observation; it is a structural one. The time horizon of a monarch is, by design, longer than that of an elected politician.

Consider the alternative. The Founders feared "the tyranny of the majority," but what we have built is the tyranny of the moment. Every four years, the United States effectively undergoes a regime change. Federal agencies are gutted or rebuilt, treaties are torn up or signed, judicial philosophies swing like pendulums, regulatory frameworks are constructed and demolished. A country cannot plant deep trees in such soil. Stability, like justice, must not only be done but must be seen to be predictably done. A monarch provides that predictability. The British system has endured, with continuous evolution, for over three centuries. American constitutional order has been tested, with grave anxieties, in every generation.

IV. Cost, Culture, and the Economy of Prestige

Critics of monarchy often cite expense. They should examine the numbers. The British royal family costs the public purse roughly £1.30 per citizen per year — a sum many Britons gladly pay, because the monarchy generates billions in tourism, soft power, and diplomatic access. The Crown Estate turns over to the Treasury vastly more than it receives. The Presidency of the United States, by contrast, costs hundreds of millions annually, and the campaigns that produce it cost billions — currently approaching ten billion dollars per cycle. This is money burned in advertising, opposition research, and political theater, producing nothing but the selection of a man or woman to live in a house and shake hands.

A monarchy is, in this sense, a public good. The British royal family is a free global broadcast service for Britishness; the Japanese Imperial House anchors Japanese identity; the Scandinavian monarchies give their small nations a gravitational center in international affairs. The United States, possessing the largest economy, the most powerful military, and the most ubiquitous popular culture in human history, has not even begun to exploit the diplomatic and economic returns such a symbolic institution could generate. An American monarchy, properly cultivated, would not be a feudal relic. It would be a strategic asset.

V. A Check on Populist Excess

The Founders feared demagogues, and gave us electoral colleges and senates. They would be horrified to see how thin these defenses have proven. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, strongmen and charlatans have repeatedly come within reach of the American presidency, armed with nothing but charisma, a slogan, and a hostile media ecosystem. The structural defenses of the Republic have not held.

A hereditary monarch provides a different kind of check: a permanent, legitimate, non-elected figure whose authority is constitutional rather than popular. In a true crisis — a contested election, a constitutional breakdown, a populist coup — a monarch can serve as a rallying point, an arbiter, a symbol of continuity that no demagogue can claim to have invented. This is not a hypothetical. The Dutch, Spanish, Belgian, and British monarchies have, in living memory, served precisely this function during wartime occupations, governmental collapses, and political crises. In the United States on January 6, 2021, there was no such figure to whom citizens of all parties could look. A monarch would have provided one.

VI. The Cultural and Educational Argument

A republic produces presidents. A monarchy produces dynasties — and dynasties, for all their flaws, are extraordinary engines of cultural formation. A prince is raised from birth to serve. He is tutored in statecraft, languages, history, the arts, diplomacy, and public duty. He travels the country not to win votes but to understand it. He is educated, in the old sense, in the literature and law of his own civilization. Compare this to the American presidential candidate of the modern era: a former senator or governor, chosen by primary voters, packaged by consultants, and tested primarily by his ability to perform in televised debates. The pool is small, the selection mechanism is crude, and the resulting figure often has no depth.

A hereditary sovereign, properly trained, accumulates over a lifetime the kind of experience, judgment, and gravitas that no four-year campaign can produce. The wisest constitutional monarchies have understood this: the King of Sweden is required to brief himself on every major area of national life; the Japanese Emperor is steeped in the history, ritual, and culture of his nation; the British monarch meets weekly with the Prime Minister and is, by long habit, the most thoroughly informed non-political figure in the realm. This is a class of leadership America has, by design, forsworn — and America is poorer for it.

VII. Addressing the Republican Counterargument

The most serious objection to monarchy in America is, of course, the principle of equality. To enthrone a family is to declare, in the words of the Declaration, that all men are not created equal. Some are born to rule; the rest are born to serve. This is a weighty objection, and it deserves a weighty answer.

The answer is that the principle of political equality need not require the abolition of all hierarchy. Judges, after all, are not elected in the way senators are. Generals are not elected at all. The Federal Reserve Chair is appointed, not chosen by the people. The Supreme Court, in its current form, gives lifetime tenure to unelected officials who wield enormous power. Americans already accept unelected, un-removable figures in crucial roles. A constitutional monarch is merely the most visible of them, and the most constrained. He does not govern. He does not legislate. He does not command armies in the field. He symbolizes, he presides, he warns, and, when necessary, he refuses to give royal assent to a course of action that would destroy the realm.

Moreover, the lived experience of modern constitutional monarchies suggests that equality and hereditary symbolism coexist comfortably. The Danes, Swedes, Norwegians, Dutch, Belgians, British, Japanese, Canadians, Australians, and New Zealanders are, by every available measure, free and equal citizens. They are also, on the whole, more contented with their political arrangements than Americans are with theirs. The contradiction the Founders feared has not materialized in any of these places.

VIII. A Practical Path Forward

Restoration need not be a coup. The American Republic could, by constitutional amendment, establish a constitutional monarchy. The amendment would define the line of succession, delineate the prerogatives of the Crown, and subordinate the elected presidency to a ceremonial prime-ministerial role. The first sovereign could be drawn from a distinguished American family — or, more plausibly, the office could be left vacant for a generation while the nation accustoms itself to the idea, the way Spain's Bourbon Restoration was negotiated after Franco. There is no historical precedent that cannot be adapted. The Americans, who have written and rewritten their constitution more than any other people, are well equipped to do so again.

IX. Conclusion: The Argument from Exhaustion

The strongest argument for American monarchy today is not romantic. It is not nostalgic. It is the argument from exhaustion. The current system demands of Americans an ever-escalating investment of attention, money, anger, and hope, and it delivers, with metronomic regularity, a head of state that half the country despises. The elections grow longer, nastier, and more expensive. The political class grows more isolated, more performative, more contemptuous of the people it claims to serve. The institutions of neutral authority — the courts, the press, the universities, the civil service — are losing legitimacy by the year.

Into this exhausted landscape, a constitutional monarch would bring three things the Republic cannot manufacture: a permanent symbol of national unity above parties, a head of state whose authority does not depend on winning a contest, and a dynasty trained from birth to embody the long view. None of these are small things. All of them are, in the most literal sense, priceless.

The Americans of 1776 overthrew a king because they had a bad one and could not get rid of him. The Americans of today have a parade of mediocre ones, and they cannot get rid of them fast enough. Perhaps it is time to remember that a crown, properly worn, can be a lighter burden than a campaign. Perhaps it is time, after two and a half centuries of restless experiment, to give the oldest and most successful form of constitutional government a serious hearing in the newest of republics.

The Founders were right to debate this question. We are wrong to have stopped.

Reestablishing a Hereditary Monarchy in the United States: A Path to Stability, Unity, and Long-Term Vision

The United States, a nation forged in the fires of revolution against hereditary monarchy, now faces persistent challenges that its founding fathers could scarcely have imagined: acute political polarization, chronic institutional gridlock, and a perpetual cycle of partisan warfare that undermines effective governance. While the current system of elected presidents has served the nation for over two centuries, its limitations grow ever more apparent in the modern age. To address these issues, Americans must consider an alternative—a constitutional hereditary monarchy. Such a system would provide a unifying, non-partisan head of state, diminish the scourge of political tribalism, and prioritize long-term national interests over short-term electoral gains. By examining the successes of modern constitutional monarchies and recognizing the structural pitfalls of the current system, this essay argues that reestablishing a hereditary monarchy could revitalize America’s democratic experiment while fostering enduring stability and prosperity.

Stability and Unity Through Neutral Leadership

Modern democratic systems often struggle with the divisiveness of elected leaders who become symbols of factional conflict. In contrast, a hereditary monarch, untethered from partisan agendas, could serve as a unifying figurehead embodying national continuity and shared identity. Just as Queen Elizabeth II provided a stabilizing presence for the United Kingdom through decades of upheaval, an American monarch could transcend the political fray, offering a consistent anchor amid the whirlwind of electoral politics. Unlike presidents whose legitimacy depends on contested votes, a monarch’s authority arises from tradition, ensuring a symbolic leader whose mandate lies in heritage rather than ephemeral popular sentiment. This neutrality could bridge ideological divides, fostering a sense of unity that democracy’s adversarial framework struggles to provide.

Breaking the Grip of Electoral Polarization

Elected presidencies in the U.S. have become battlegrounds where candidates weaponize divisive rhetoric to mobilize their base, often at the expense of pragmatic compromise. The 2020 election and its aftermath exemplified how partisan animosity can escalate into social unrest, threatening the very fabric of democracy. A constitutional monarch, however, would be above such fray. By removing the presidency from the electoral arena, the nation could redirect focus toward issues rather than personalities, reducing the incentives for demagoguery. This reform would not abolish democracy but would eliminate one of its most bitterly contested offices, allowing Congress and state governments to operate with less acrimony while empowering a neutral figure to champion national cohesion.

Long-Term Vision Over Short-Term Gains

Elected presidents are often constrained by the "tyranny of the next election," compelled to prioritize immediate wins over enduring solutions. Climate change, infrastructure decay, and educational reform languish while leaders obsess over re-election cycles. A monarch, by contrast, could pursue policies with generational impact, such as sustainable environmental strategies or debt reduction, unshackled from the need to placate campaign donors or swing-state voters. This long-term perspective would transform governance from a reactive, poll-driven process into a proactive, visionary endeavor. Like the emperors of Japan, who have long championed cultural and environmental stewardship, an American monarch could institutionalize strategic thinking that benefits future citizens, not just upcoming election cycles.

Institutional Harmony and Consensus Building

The U.S. presidency wields significant executive power, often leading to clashes with Congress and the judiciary. These confrontations stall progress and erode public trust in governmental institutions. A constitutional monarch could mediate these conflicts more effectively, leveraging ceremonial authority to encourage collaboration. In the United Kingdom, the monarch acts as a non-partisan figure who convenes Parliament, symbolizing unity while allowing elected officials to debate freely. Adopting a similar model in America might reduce gridlock, encouraging legislators to prioritize national welfare over partisan advantage. Furthermore, the monarch could appoint prime ministers or cabinet members based on merit, not electoral victory, ensuring competent governance even in turbulent times.

Cultural Identity and Economic Advantages

Monarchies often serve as repositories of national heritage, cultivating traditions that instill pride and continuity. A royal family could promote American values through ceremonial events and cultural initiatives, reinforcing civic identity in an era of globalization’s homogenizing forces. Additionally, the elimination of costly presidential campaigns would reduce the corrupting influence of money in politics. In 2020, over $14 billion was spent on federal elections—a figure that could instead fund public education or technological innovation. Finally, constitutional monarchies like Sweden and Norway consistently rank among the world’s happiest and most economically stable nations, suggesting that such systems can coexist with prosperity, environmental stewardship, and social equity.

Addressing Counterarguments: Legitimacy, Competence, and Democracy

Critics might argue that hereditary rule undermines democratic agency, but a constitutional monarch’s powers could be strictly limited, maintaining democratic supremacy in legislative and judicial realms. Just as the British monarch’s role is largely ceremonial, an American sovereign could embody national unity while leaving practical governance to elected bodies. Questions of competence could be mitigated by rigorous education and training for royal heirs, ensuring preparedness; indeed, many modern royals hold advanced degrees and have demonstrated leadership acumen. Furthermore, the current system already permits unqualified leaders to ascend via gerrymandering, voter suppression, or media manipulation—a problem monarchy would eradicate entirely.

Conclusion: A Timely Revival of Tested Wisdom

America’s experiment with elected executive leadership has reached an inflection point. The relentless churn of campaigns, the erosion of civility in public discourse, and the prioritization of short-term tactics over long-term strategies all signal a need for transformation. A hereditary monarchy would not discard democracy but would refine it, offering stability, unity, and vision that elected leaders often cannot. By learning from constitutional monarchies worldwide, the United States could forge a hybrid system where elected representatives govern day-to-day, while a hereditary sovereign ensures enduring national purpose and cohesion. This is not a call to return to the past but a bold step into a future where leadership transcends partisanship, governance prioritizes the public good, and America’s democratic ideals are preserved with renewed vigor and wisdom.

The Case for a Constitutional Monarchy in America

An Argument for Long-Term Stability Over the Chaos of Permanent Campaigns

Introduction

At first blush, the suggestion that the United States should adopt a hereditary monarchy sounds like satire, provocation, or a particularly poor reading of American history. The republic was founded in explicit revolt against a king. The Declaration of Independence catalogued grievances against George III with an almost prosecutorial zeal. The Constitution distributed power precisely to prevent its concentration in a single permanent officeholder. And yet — with respect to the founders — political arrangements are tools, not sacred relics. If a constitutional monarchy could address deep structural dysfunctions that the current system has proven unable or unwilling to solve, then intellectual honesty demands the argument be heard, even if it is ultimately rejected.

This essay will argue, seriously and in detail, that replacing the American presidency with a hereditary constitutional monarch — a non-partisan, ceremonial-but-symbolically-powerful head of state — would produce a more stable, more unified, and more effectively governed nation. It will draw on comparative evidence from existing constitutional monarchies, diagnose specific pathologies of the American system, and respond to the most obvious objections.

I. The Problem: What the Presidency Has Become

To make the affirmative case, one must first be honest about what the modern American presidency actually is, as opposed to what the founders designed or what civic textbooks describe.

The presidency has become a quasi-monarchical office without any of the advantages of monarchy. The president is simultaneously head of state, head of government, commander-in-chief, chief diplomat, party leader, legislative agenda-setter, cultural symbol, and — increasingly — a figure around whom an entire national identity coalesces or fractures. This is an extraordinary concentration of formal and informal power.

At the same time, the president is a partisan figure, elected through a process that now runs continuously. The moment a president takes office, campaigning for the next cycle begins. Every action is filtered through its effect on re-election or on the party's prospects. The president governs for the roughly half of the country that voted for them and is structurally incentivized to treat the other half as an obstacle or an enemy.

The result is a head of state who cannot unify, because unification is not the currency of the system that selected them. The currency is division. You win by mobilizing your base, not by appealing to the whole. The president is thus a permanent partisan combatant who is also supposed to be the symbolic embodiment of the entire nation — a contradiction that grows more unmanageable with every passing decade.

Hereditary monarchy resolves this contradiction by permanently separating the roles of head of state (the symbol of unity, continuity, and national identity) from head of government (the partisan political leader who actually governs and can be removed).

II. The Comparative Evidence: Constitutional Monarchies Outperform

This is not a purely theoretical argument. We have extensive comparative data, and it overwhelmingly favors constitutional monarchies on measures that Americans say they care about.

Political stability. Of the top twenty most politically stable nations in the world as measured by the Economist Intelligence Unit's Democracy Index and the Fragile States Index, a striking number are constitutional monarchies: Norway, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Luxembourg, Belgium, the United Kingdom, and Spain. These are not relics of feudalism hanging on through inertia; they are among the most prosperous, free, democratically governed, and socially cohesive societies on earth.

Democratic quality. The same monarchies consistently rank higher than the United States on measures of democratic health — press freedom, voter participation, trust in institutions, absence of corruption, and civil liberties. The idea that monarchy and democracy are opposites is empirically false. Constitutional monarchy, far from undermining democracy, appears to strengthen it by relieving democratic institutions of the burden of also serving as the nation's symbolic and emotional core.

Social trust and cohesion. Citizens of constitutional monarchies report significantly higher levels of social trust and national belonging. A monarch who belongs to no party can, in moments of genuine crisis, speak to the entire nation in a way that an elected partisan simply cannot. When Queen Elizabeth II addressed the United Kingdom during COVID-19, she spoke not as a Conservative or a Labour figure but as the Queen — a symbol shared by everyone. No American president, no matter how skilled, can do this, because everyone knows which party they represent.

Why does this work? Political scientists offer several explanations:

  1. The "dignified vs. efficient" distinction (Walter Bagehot): The monarchy handles the symbolic, ceremonial, and unifying functions of government, allowing elected politicians to focus on the messy, contentious work of actual governance.
  2. Removal of the cult of personality from democratic politics: When the nation's ultimate symbol is hereditary and apolitical, elected leaders are more easily understood as servants and employees, not as quasi-sacred figures. This actually makes it easier to hold them accountable.
  3. Stability of national identity: A monarch provides a continuous thread of national identity that survives changes in government. In the United States, the presidency is so central to national identity that a change in president can feel like a change in what the country is.

III. Specific Structural Advantages

A. Ending the Permanent Campaign

The American political system now operates in a state of permanent electoral warfare. Presidential campaigns begin two or more years before the election. Midterm elections function as referenda on the president. Every policy debate is a campaign event. The result is governance by spectacle, short-termism, and strategic outrage.

A hereditary monarch eliminates the need to elect a head of state entirely. The nation's symbolic leader is simply there, providing continuity. This allows the political system to focus on governance rather than perpetual electoral competition. The head of government (a prime minister or equivalent) can be replaced through normal parliamentary mechanisms without triggering an existential national crisis about the identity of the country.

B. Genuine Non-Partisan National Leadership

The United States currently has no non-partisan national figure. The Chief Justice comes closest but is identified with a judicial philosophy. The president is obviously partisan. Congressional leaders are partisan. There is no one who can speak for all Americans without half the country immediately discounting their words as political maneuvering.

A monarch fills this vacuum. When the king or queen visits a disaster zone, speaks at a memorial, or addresses the nation in a moment of grief, their words carry a weight that is uncontaminated by partisanship. This is not a trivial function. It is, in fact, one of the most important things a government can provide: a sense that the nation is more than its political disagreements.

C. Reducing the Imperial Presidency

Ironically, introducing a monarch might reduce the concentration of power that currently makes the presidency so dangerous. Under the current system, the president accumulates both symbolic authority (the emotional loyalty of their supporters) and executive authority (the formal powers of the office). This combination is what makes the presidency imperial.

Separating these functions means that the head of government (the prime minister or equivalent) would hold executive power without the symbolic aura of the head of state. They would be understood as a political functionary — powerful, but removable, replaceable, and not the embodiment of the nation. This would make it psychologically and politically easier to constrain their power, challenge their decisions, and remove them from office.

D. Institutional Memory and Long-Term Perspective

Elected leaders operate on two-year, four-year, and six-year time horizons. Monarchs operate on generational time horizons. A monarch who expects to reign for decades — and who will pass the throne to their children — has an inherent incentive to think about the long-term health of the nation, the stability of its institutions, and the welfare of future generations. This is precisely the kind of thinking that democratic politics, by its nature, struggles to produce.

Queen Elizabeth II reigned for seventy years. During that time, she had audiences with fifteen British prime ministers. She saw policy fashions come and go. She provided a perspective on institutional continuity that no elected official, limited by term and ambition, could match. The United States, facing long-term challenges like climate change, fiscal sustainability, and social fragmentation, could benefit enormously from an institution capable of thinking beyond the next election cycle.

IV. Addressing the Objections

"But the founders rejected monarchy!"

Elected presidents serve brief terms, creating policy whiplash as each administration reverses its predecessor. The British, Dutch, Scandinavian, and Japanese monarchies demonstrate that constitutional kings and queens can coexist with vibrant democracies while providing apolitical stability.

The dignified part inspires loyalty and unifies the nation; the efficient part actually governs. America has crammed both into one office, overburdening it. Introduction

The American presidency was designed to be a unifying figure, a leader who would rise above factionalism and represent the entire nation. Yet, in practice, the modern presidency has become the opposite: a hyper-partisan office where every election is treated as an existential battle, where incumbents are constantly campaigning rather than governing, and where the legitimacy of the office itself is frequently called into question.

The process consumes billions of dollars, dominates political discourse, and leaves the nation deeply split. The Founding Fathers envisioned a presidency that would be above partisan squabbling, yet today, the office is the most politicized institution in America. Presidents are expected to be both head of state (a symbolic, unifying figure) and head of government (a political leader). This dual role creates inherent conflicts. When a president gives a speech, is it meant to inspire national unity or to advance a partisan agenda? When they attend a state funeral, are they representing the nation or their political base?

A constitutional monarchy resolves this dilemma by separating the two roles. The monarch serves as the apolitical head of state—embodying national identity, continuity, and tradition—while an elected prime minister (or a reformed Congress) handles the day-to-day governance. This division exists successfully in nations like the United Kingdom, Canada, and Japan, where the monarch provides stability while politicians debate policy.

3. The Problem of Term Limits and Lame Ducks

The U.S. presidency is hamstrung by term limits, which create "lame duck" periods where presidents lose influence in their final years. This weakens governance and encourages short-term thinking, as presidents prioritize reelection or legacy over long-term planning. A hereditary monarch, serving for life, would provide consistency in leadership, ensuring that national institutions remain stable regardless of political shifts.

1. Stability in an Age of Chaos

Democracies are prone to sudden shifts in leadership, often driven by populist waves or political exhaustion. The United States has seen presidents impeached, elections contested, and transitions of power marred by violence (as in the January 6 Capitol riot). America, lacking such a figure, often sees its presidency become a lightning rod for division rather than a source of unity.

One of the greatest strengths of a monarchy is its ability to transcend politics. The monarch represents the nation as a whole, not just a faction. Donald Trump was the "Republican president," Joe Biden the "Democratic president"—each viewed with suspicion by the opposition.

A monarch, however, belongs to no party. They do not campaign, they do not legislate, and they do not take sides in political disputes. Their role is to embody the nation’s history, values, and continuity. This is why monarchies often have higher approval ratings than elected leaders—because they are not tainted by partisan warfare.

Elected leaders operate on short time horizons, driven by the next election cycle. This encourages policies that yield quick political wins rather than long-term benefits. A monarchy, by contrast, thinks in generations. In the U.S., the lack of institutional memory at the highest level contributes to policy whiplash—each new administration reverses the last, creating instability in foreign policy, economic regulation, and social programs. A monarch, serving for life, would provide a counterbalance to this trend, ensuring that some elements of governance remain consistent regardless of political shifts.

America was founded in part as a rejection of monarchy, but that rejection was rooted in the abuses of absolute rule—not in the concept of hereditary leadership itself. Many of the Founding Fathers, including Alexander Hamilton, admired the British constitutional monarchy and saw value in a strong, stable executive. Over time, however, the presidency has become more imperial than any king, with expansive powers that were never intended.

The monarch would have no political power; real governance would remain with elected officials. Constitutional monarchies have safeguards against abuse. The monarch’s powers would be strictly ceremonial, with real authority resting in Congress and the courts. Elections are increasingly contentious, legitimacy is constantly questioned, and the nation lurches from one political extreme to another with no sense of continuity. A hereditary monarchy would not solve all of America’s problems, but it would provide what the nation lacks most: stability, unity, and a head of state who belongs to all citizens, not just those who voted for them.

Far from being a regressive step, a constitutional monarchy would modernize American governance by separating the ceremonial and political functions of leadership. It would reduce the toxic polarization of presidential elections, ensure long-term thinking in governance, and restore a sense of national identity that transcends partisan divides. The time has come to reconsider the wisdom of the Founders—not by abandoning democracy, but by perfecting it with an institution that has stood the test of time. America should crown a king.

1. Stability and Continuity

One of the greatest weaknesses of the presidential system is its inherent discontinuity. Every four or eight years, the nation undergoes a potentially jarring transition of power. Policies are reversed, international agreements renegotiated, and the bureaucracy redirected—all at the whim of the electorate. This constant churn breeds uncertainty at home and abroad, making long‑term planning difficult for both businesses and government. Consider Queen Elizabeth II, whose 70‑year reign gave the United Kingdom a rock of stability through war, decolonization, economic crises, and social transformation. The mere presence of a monarch who transcends electoral cycles creates an atmosphere of permanence and reliability—qualities sorely lacking in today’s America.

2. A Non‑Partisan Unifying Figure

The President of the United States is inevitably a partisan figure. Elected on a party ticket, he or she embodies the agenda of one faction and is viewed with suspicion, if not outright hostility, by the opposing side. This deepens societal rifts and undermines the idea of a shared national identity. A constitutional monarch, however, stands above politics. Sworn to serve all citizens equally, the monarch can be a unifying symbol, representing the nation as a whole rather than a narrow majority. In countries like Sweden and the Netherlands, royal birthdays and addresses are occasions for national celebration, not division. The monarch’s role in state ceremonies, from the opening of parliament to the signing of legislation, is performed without partisan bias, lending dignity and legitimacy to the democratic process. By removing politics from the head of state, America could begin to heal its bitter partisan wounds.

Presidential elections are astronomically expensive, socially divisive, and incredibly time‑consuming. The 2020 election cycle cost over $14 billion, money that could have been spent on infrastructure, education, or healthcare. Moreover, the years‑long campaign distracts elected officials from governing and forces candidates to make unrealistic promises to win votes. A hereditary monarchy eliminates these costs and distractions. The British royal family, for example, generates an estimated £1.8 billion annually for the U.K. economy through tourism and media. Even if an American monarchy incurred similar costs, it would still be a bargain compared to the billions wasted every four years on political campaigns that leave half the country feeling alienated.

4. Historical and Cultural Resonance

It is true that the United States was born out of a revolution against a tyrannical king. But that king, George III, ruled an absolute monarchy in an age when the very idea of constitutional limits was in its infancy. Today’s constitutional monarchies are among the most democratic, prosperous, and free societies on earth. Critics will charge that monarchy is inherently undemocratic. But in a constitutional monarchy, the monarch’s powers are strictly limited by law and tradition. Real executive authority resides with an elected prime minister and parliament, while the monarch performs ceremonial duties and serves as a check on extreme partisanship (e.g., by appointing a government when elections are inconclusive). The United States could adopt a similar model: retain the Congress and the Supreme Court, but replace the presidency with a ceremonial monarch and a prime minister chosen from the majority in the House of Representatives. This would preserve the separation of powers and democratic accountability while adding a stabilizing, non‑partisan element at the apex of the state. Hereditary privilege: It is undeniably unfair that one family is born into privilege. Yet many aspects of society—wealth, social status, even political dynasties—are already hereditary. The process itself would force Americans to reexamine their assumptions about government and to envision a future where unity triumphs over division. The time has come to consider the unthinkable: a new American monarchy for a new American century.

In the words of the great statesman Winston Churchill, “Democracy is the worst form of government except all those other forms that have been tried.” But even Churchill, a lifelong democrat, served under a constitutional monarch and understood the value of a non‑political head of state. The United States has tried the presidential system for over two centuries; while it has served well in many respects, its flaws have become increasingly apparent. By adopting a hereditary monarchy, America would not abandon its democratic heritage but would refine it, adding an element of continuity and unity that the presidency can never provide. Introduction

The United States of America was born in rebellion against monarchy, its founders fearing tyranny and embracing republican ideals.
