I. Historical Precedents: Monarchies Outlast Republics

A brief survey of global history reveals that monarchies have often provided greater stability than republics, particularly in large and diverse nations. The United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, and the Scandinavian monarchies have endured for centuries with minimal political disruption, whereas many republics—including those of Latin America, Weimar Germany, and numerous African and Asian states—have suffered coups, civil strife, and institutional collapse.

A. The Stability of Constitutional Monarchies

Constitutional monarchies, where the monarch reigns but does not rule, have proven remarkably resilient. Examples include:

  • The United Kingdom: Despite political turmoil (World Wars, decolonization, Brexit), the monarchy has remained a constant symbol of national unity.
  • Japan: The Emperor, having renounced political power after World War II, serves as a unifying figure without the destructive partisan battles seen in presidential systems.
  • Scandinavia: Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have some of the world’s most stable democracies, with monarchies that enhance rather than detract from governance.

In contrast, the U.S. has experienced violent power transitions (e.g., the assassination of Abraham Lincoln, the near-assassination of Ronald Reagan, and the Jan. 6 Capitol riot) and chronic governmental dysfunction. The 24/7 news cycle, partisan polarization, and the two-term limit (which eliminates institutional memory) make the presidency a revolving door of short-term leadership, whereas a hereditary monarch provides continuity.

B. The Failure of Presidential Republics

Many presidential republics have collapsed into dictatorship or anarchy. Consider:

  • Latin America: From the violent coups of the 20th century to the populist strongmen of the 21st (e.g., Chavez, Bolsonaro), many presidential systems have struggled with instability.
  • France’s Fifth Republic: While France’s semi-presidential system has functioned, it has still seen protests, strikes, and political paralysis (e.g., the Yellow Vests movement).
  • The United States: The presidency, originally designed as a limited executive, has become an imperial office—with presidents wielding unprecedented war powers, executive orders, and partisan influence over the judiciary.

A hereditary monarchy would not suffer from term limits, campaign financing, or the destructive pressures of re-election—factors that distort policy in presidential systems.

II. The Non-Partisan Advantage: A Monarch as Unifying Symbol

One of the greatest weaknesses of the U.S. presidency is its inherent partisanship. Presidents are elected as representatives of political parties, forcing them to govern in a polarized manner. A monarch, however, is fundamentally above politics.

A. Removing the Partisan Presidency

  • The presidency is now a hyper-partisan office, with each administration reversing or undermining the policies of its predecessor (e.g., healthcare, climate regulations, foreign policy swings).

  • The British monarchy, for example, reinforces a sense of shared history and tradition. The U.S. lacks such a symbol—its last constitutional monarch (King George III) was overthrown in 1776.
  • A new American monarchy could draw from both European traditions and home-grown legends (e.g., incorporating Native American, African American, and immigrant narratives into its legitimacy).

III. Economic and Governance Benefits

A hereditary monarchy would not only stabilize politics but also improve governance and economic confidence.

A. Eliminating the "Election Economy"

  • The U.S. spends billions on presidential elections every four years, with constant fundraising and campaigning distracting from governance.

  • The monarchy could serve as a stabilizing force during economic crises, much like Queen Elizabeth II did during Brexit and the 2008 financial crash.

C. Avoiding Presidential Succession Crises

  • Presidential elections create massive uncertainty—what if a candidate dies or is incapacitated before taking office? (See: 1876, 1968, 2020 controversies.)
  • A hereditary line eliminates this risk. The royal family would be trained from birth for the role, ensuring competency.

IV. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

  • Rebuttal: A constitutional monarchy is not absolute tyranny—it is a system where the monarch’s role is ceremonial, with elected officials handling governance. The UK, Canada, and Japan are among the freest nations in the world, yet they retain monarchies.

  • Rebuttal: Public opinion shifts—just as American attitudes toward monarchy changed after 1776. Many Americans already admire figures like Queen Elizabeth II, and a modern constitutional monarchy could be framed as a "renewed covenant" with a new national symbol.
  • The U.S. already has elements of monarchy (e.g., lifetime Supreme Court justices, the "imperial presidency," and the cult of the flag and anthem). A formal monarchy would merely codify what already exists in practice.

Conclusion: A New American Monarchy for a New Era

The United States was founded on revolutionary ideals, but revolutions are not immune to evolution. The presidential system, once a bold experiment, has become a source of instability, corruption, and division. In an age of deep polarization, climate crises, and global power struggles, America needs a head of state who is above politics—a symbol of unity rather than a partisan warrior.

  3. Unify the nation under a shared symbol of tradition and history.

  5. Strengthen economic and governance stability by removing the economic and administrative burdens of constant elections.

A constitutional monarchy could transform America from a nation of fleeting presidencies and endless partisan warfare into a dignified, stable, and united power—one that commands respect not through intimidation, but through grace.

The time has come to recolonize America—not with swords and crowns, but with wisdom and continuity. Long live the American monarch.
